strengths: Thoughtfully designed asymmetric cross-modal interaction mechanism that balances convergence speed and contextual information through modality-specific A2V and V2A aligners

Comprehensive evaluation framework across audio quality, video quality, and audio-video consistency metrics with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test cases
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3, Figures 5-7) systematically validating each architectural component and training strategy

Incomplete technical analysis: no inference computational cost/speed reported, MA-CFG coefficients s_v and s_a lack ablation, lip-sync only via SyncNet without human assessment, sensitivity to hyperparameters unexplored

Comprehensive system design with well-motivated architectural components and clear presentation of the overall framework
Extensive ablation studies examining individual contributions of key components (cross-modal interaction, FAM, MA-CFG, training strategies)
Evaluation across multiple dimensions: audio quality, video quality, and audio-video consistency metrics
Demonstrates some generalization capability with mixed in-distribution and OOD (anime) domain evaluation

Weak reproducibility: training data is private and not publicly available, making reproduction impossible; no code release mentioned; complex three-stage training procedure with many unexplained hyperparameters

Questionable comparative advantage over concurrent work: modest/inconsistent improvements over Ovi (e.g., LS score 5.95 vs 6.48 where higher is better; Dynamic Degree is comparable), no fair comparison with controlled training data amounts across methods

Insufficient justification for core design choices: why the specific asymmetry (context window for A2V but interpolation for V2A)? Missing ablations on context window size (w) and audio-to-video token ratio (k); unclear why Stage 1 audio-only pre-training is necessary

Generalization claims lack rigorous support: OOD claim based on single anime example without systematic evaluation; limited to English speech; no multilingual or accent diversity testing despite using multilingual dataset

Ablation studies use suboptimal protocol: results default to 'first 10k steps of Stage 2' rather than full training, potentially misrepresenting final performance trends; no ablation on three-stage training necessity or λ_m decay schedule

Missing statistical rigor: no significance testing or error bars on reported metrics; hyperparameter choices (e.g., task ratio 4:1:1:2:2) lack justification; Figure 6 shows visual improvements with MA-CFG but provides no quantitative numbers

Limited qualitative evidence: only two visual examples provided; no failure case analysis; no discussion of limitations when handling videos with multiple speakers, extreme conditions, or non-facial audio

Incomplete technical analysis: asymmetry described as achieving 'superior balance' but lacks formal justification; why this architecture is optimal compared to alternatives unexplored; computational costs (training time, inference latency, memory) not discussed

No user studies despite focus on synchronization and emotional consistency where human perception is critical; results rely entirely on automated metrics

Reproducibility concerns: internally collected training dataset for Stage 2/3 not characterized (size, quality, accessibility); no code/model release plans mentioned; cannot fully verify experimental setup
Missing critical technical details: window size w for A2V context not specified, λm decay schedule undefined, task ratio selection (4:1:1:2:2) unjustified with no ablation study

No failure case analysis, no evaluation of content type performance variation, no computational cost comparisons, and missing sensitivity analyses (window size w, interpolation granularity, mask threshold effects)
Marginal improvements on some metrics: lip-sync (5.95 vs 6.48 for Ovi is worse), and some ablation improvements are small (Table 3: unsupervised FAM shows minimal difference from supervised)

Impressive data efficiency: competitive results with 1.3M training samples versus 30.7M for competitors, suggesting effective architectural design

Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3, 7-9), qualitative comparisons showing out-of-distribution generalization (anime inputs), and user study with 34 participants
Careful technical execution with thoughtful handling of temporal alignment, context windows, and component insertion positions; clear mathematical formulations
Effective presentation with informative figures, particularly Figure 3's conceptual comparison of interaction mechanisms

Major reproducibility limitations: private training dataset (Stage 2) prevents verification and fair comparison; reliance on proprietary Wan models for backbone; proprietary evaluation tools; no mentioned code/model release despite claims of addressing open-source limitations

Constrained scope limiting generality: single-speaker human-centric only; cannot handle multi-person scenarios or ambient sounds; acknowledged but significantly narrows applicability compared to general audio-video generation claims

Inconsistent quantitative results undercutting main claims: UniAVGen underperforms Ovi on lip-sync (LS: 5.95 vs 6.48) despite synchronized generation claims; public benchmark results (Tables 5-6) show near-SOTA rather than clear superiority

Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies (main + supplementary), qualitative examples, and user studies demonstrating systematic component analysis
Elegant multi-task unification framework handling five related tasks within a single model without task-specific designs

Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figure 3 effectively compares interaction mechanisms)
weaknesses: Critical evaluation validity issues: Timbre (TC) and Emotion Consistency (EC)—claimed as primary advantages—rely on unreliable LLM-based metrics without human inter-rater reliability studies; reported improvements are marginal (TC: 0.832 vs 0.828 for Ovi) within typical LLM noise
Insufficient test scale (only 100 samples, 50 in-distribution/50 OOD) limits statistical significance for generalization claims

Limited technical novelty: components are standard (cross-attention windows, temporal interpolation, soft masking) with contribution primarily in their combination—more engineering than conceptual innovation

Unfair comparison with concurrent methods: Ovi trained on 30.7M samples vs UniAVGen's 1.3M, confounding data quantity with method quality; two-stage baselines use F5-TTS (not intended for this pipeline)
Complex three-stage training procedure lacks ablation: no comparison with end-to-end joint training; task ratio (4:1:1:2:2) not ablated; design justification incomplete

Severe reproducibility limitations: private dataset without specification, no released code, underspecified hyperparameters (context window w=0.5, decay schedules, CFG coefficients s_v=3, s_a=2 empirically set without ablation)

Metric selection bias: Dynamic Degree naturally favors generated motion over static video; selection emphasizes metrics where method excels (timbre via LLM) while marginal on standard metrics (LS: 5.95 vs Ovi 6.48)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical limitations of decoupled audio-video generation pipelines; clear identification of why existing methods fail at cross-modal synchronization

Impressive data efficiency: achieves competitive results with 1.3M samples vs. 30.7M for Ovi, with strong generalization to out-of-distribution domains (anime images)
Practical unified framework supporting 5 distinct audio-video tasks within a single model with demonstrated multi-task learning benefits

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions (audio quality, video quality, audio-video consistency), detailed ablation studies (Tables 2-3, 7-9), and user study validation (34 participants, Table 4)
Face-Aware Modulation is well-motivated for human-centric generation, with clear empirical validation of the decaying supervision strategy (Table 3, Figure 5)
Modality-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance is a novel extension of CFG specifically designed for joint generation that effectively amplifies cross-modal dependencies
Excellent presentation quality with clear figures, well-structured arguments, and detailed supplementary materials including extended ablations and additional benchmarks
weaknesses: Critical evaluation methodology concern: Timbre Consistency (TC) and Emotion Consistency (EC)—central to the paper's claims—rely exclusively on commercial LLM (Gemini-2.5-Pro) evaluation without human validation; LLM evaluations lack reliability guarantees and are susceptible to prompt engineering bias; only 3 independent evaluations reported is insufficient to address validity concerns

Severely limited reproducibility: internal proprietary dataset with no public access, undisclosed size and composition, complex 3-stage training procedure with multiple unjustified hyperparameters, no code or model release mentioned; restricts independent verification and community building

Small test set (only 100 custom-created samples) potentially subject to unintended biases; lack of evaluation on established joint audio-video generation benchmarks makes relative performance assessment difficult; no on-distribution benchmark evaluation for joint generation task

Baseline comparison limitations: two-stage methods use different pipeline (F5-TTS preprocessing), limiting direct comparability; Ovi is concurrent work; missing comparisons with other recent joint generation methods mentioned in related work

Limited architectural novelty: directly reuses Wan 2.2-5B and Wan 2.1-1.3B as backbones with main novelty concentrated in interaction mechanisms rather than core generative models; improvements over Ovi could be partially attributable to implementation details

Insufficient justification for design choices: audio context window w=1/2 (Sec. 6.1) lacks ablation or principled motivation; V2A interpolation factor α=(j mod k)/k appears arbitrary; zero-initialization of output matrices treated as workaround without exploring alternatives; CFG interval [0.5, 1] justified only empirically

Face-Aware Modulation scope limitations: core assumption that facial regions dominate synchronization may not generalize beyond human speech to body-centric expressions, music videos, or non-human subjects; decaying λm schedule is ad-hoc without principled decay strategy

Incomplete multi-task learning analysis: improvement from multi-task training (Fig. 7) is modest (~0.3 LC metric); no breakdown of which tasks contribute most; limited investigation of task interference or synergistic effects

Practical deployment considerations unaddressed: no inference time comparison with baselines; MA-CFG overhead from additional forward passes not reported; training complexity (3-stage procedure) not thoroughly justified

Limited failure mode analysis: Section 11 acknowledges lack of ambient sound generation and multi-person constraints, but systematic analysis of when and why the model fails is absent; no discussion of performance on accents, unusual expressions, or out-of-domain speakers
